4c(1).fact: Senders must return both flags downward to the rest position after each word so the receiver can distinguish word boundaries.
4c(1).misconception: Signalers can transmit a complete sentence continuously without pausing or resetting their flags between individual words.
4c(1).pamphlet_summary: Signaling requires holding two flags with arms fully extended along precise clock angles while facing the receiver directly. Senders must drop both flags to the rest position across the lower body to mark the completion of each word (p. 21).
4c(1).socratic_question: If you are watching a sender transmit a ten-word sentence across an open field, how would you distinguish where one word ends and the next begins?

4c(2).fact: Individual nautical flags have standardized international meanings that convey immediate navigational status and emergency warnings without spelling words.
4c(2).misconception: Nautical flags function solely as an alphabet to spell out written words letter by letter.
4c(2).pamphlet_summary: The International Code of Signals uses standardized geometric patterns and high-contrast colors across forty distinct flags, including letters, numerals, and pennants. Ships hoist these flags individually for urgent safety warnings, such as notifying nearby vessels of divers in the water or hazardous cargo, or in combinations to transmit complex navigational messages (p. 26).
4c(2).socratic_question: Why does international maritime law assign complete emergency meanings to single flags rather than requiring crews to spell out every warning letter by letter?
